en: Parivāra Cūḷasaṅgāma 14.
The Conduct of an Investigator (Anuvijjaka)
A monk who dwells in the midst of battle, when approaching the Saṅgha,
should approach the Saṅgha with a humble mind,
with a mind like a dust-sweeper.
One should be skilled in sitting and skilled in posture; one should not encroach upon senior bhikkhus, nor should one obstruct junior bhikkhus from taking a seat.

One should sit on a seat that is appropriate. One should not be a chatterer, nor one who indulges in frivolous talk. Either one should speak the Dhamma oneself, or request another to do so; or else, the noble silence should not be disregarded.
When one wishes to investigate with the approval of the Saṅgha as an investigator, one need not ask one’s preceptor.
One should not ask about the teacher, one should not ask about the co-resident, one should not ask about the pupil,
one should not ask about the co-superior, one should not ask about the co-teacher, one should not ask about birth, one should not ask about the name,
one should not ask about the clan, one should not ask about the place of origin, nor about the family lineage.
He should be questioned, but his native land should not be questioned.
For what reason?
Because he might have affection for it or hatred toward it.
When there is affection or when there is hatred, one might act out of favoritism, one might act out of hatred, one might act out of delusion, or one might act out of fear.
A person who has been authorized by the Sangha as an investigator and who desires to investigate must respect the Sangha rather than respecting an individual;
he must respect the true Dhamma rather than respecting material gain; he must be devoted to what is beneficial.
One should not be a partisan of one's own faction; one should investigate at the proper time, not at an improper time; one should investigate based on what is factual, not on what is unfactual;
one should investigate gently, not harshly; one should investigate with what is beneficial, not with what is harmful;
one should investigate with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner ill will; and one should not whisper into the ear.
One should be composed; one should not look askance, nor stare with fixed eyes, nor raise the eyebrows, nor nod the head, nor make gestures with the hands, nor display hand-signs.
One should be skilled in sitting and skilled in posture, looking only the distance of a plough-yoke and conforming to the purpose.
One should sit on one's own seat; one should not rise from the seat, nor shift about, nor take a by-path, nor speak with gesticulating arms.

One should be unhurried and free from rashness; one should be without impetuosity, patient in speech, possessed of a mind of loving-kindness, compassionate and seeking the welfare of others; one should be merciful and intent upon the well-being of those around.
One should be free from frivolous speech and moderate in talk; one should be free from enmity and without malice.
One should examine oneself and examine others; one should examine the accuser and the accused;
one should examine the one who accuses unrighteously and the one who is accused unrighteously; and one should examine the one who accuses righteously.

One who has been censured according to the Dhamma should be examined: by not letting what was said go unaddressed and by clarifying what was not said, one should carefully examine the words and phrases of the offense, question the other person, and deal with them according to their admission;

one who is dull-witted should be encouraged, one who is timid should be reassured, one who is fierce should be restrained, and one who is impure should be made to reveal it; with straightforward gentleness, one should not follow a course of action out of favoritism.
One should proceed; one should not proceed with a course of hatred, nor with a course of delusion, nor with a course of fear.
One should remain impartial toward both phenomena and persons.

And when an investigator investigates in this manner, he acts in accordance with the Teacher’s instruction; he becomes dear, agreeable, respected, and esteemed by wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life.
The discourse is for the purpose of connecting; the simile is for the purpose of illustration; the meaning is for the purpose of making known; the counter-question is for the purpose of establishing;
the granting of an opportunity is for the purpose of reproving; the reproving is for the purpose of reminding; the reminding is for the purpose of making one speak;
the speaking is for the purpose of creating an obstacle; the obstacle is for the purpose of adjudication; the adjudication is for the purpose of investigation.

Investigation is for the purpose of discerning what is possible and what is impossible; the discernment of what is possible and what is impossible is for the purpose of restraining individuals who are difficult to manage and for the purpose of supporting well-behaved monks; the Saṅgha is for the purpose of receiving and accepting [those individuals];
and individuals approved by the Saṅgha are for the purpose of acting independently and being non-deceptive.

The Vinaya is for the purpose of restraint; restraint is for the purpose of non-remorse; non-remorse is for the purpose of gladness; gladness is for the purpose of rapture; rapture is for the purpose of tranquility;
tranquility is for the purpose of happiness; happiness is for the purpose of concentration;

concentration is for the purpose of knowing and seeing things as they truly are; knowing and seeing things as they truly are is for the purpose of disenchantment; disenchantment is for the purpose of dispassion.

Dispassion is for the sake of liberation; liberation is for the sake of the knowledge and vision of liberation; the knowledge and vision of liberation is for the sake of final Nibbāna through non-clinging.
This is the purpose of discourse, this is the purpose of consultation, this is the purpose of support, this is the purpose of lending an ear:
namely, the liberation of the mind through non-clinging.
Listen to the practice of the duties,
performed by one who is wise and skilled;
it is well-spoken and in accordance with the training rules.
One who is unskilled in the destination in the life to come,
in the basis, the failure, the offense,
the cause, and the mode.
He does not know what comes before or after,
nor what has been done or left undone, nor what is equitable;
he knows neither formal acts nor legal issues.
And being unskilled even in serenity,
impassioned, corrupted, and deluded,
he proceeds out of fear and out of delusion.
Not skilled in conciliation,
unskilled in reconciliation,
having gained a faction, he is shameless.
One who performs black deeds and is disrespectful—
such a bhikkhu is indeed called "one who does not turn back."
One who is skilled in the subject matter, the failure, the offense,
the cause, and the modes,
and who knows what precedes and follows—
What has been done and what has not been done, as well as the equal [treatment];
skilled in action, in legal issues,
and also in the methods of settling them.
Free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion,
he does not go [astray] out of fear or confusion;
he is skilled in persuasion.
Skilled in self-satisfaction,
having gained a following, modest,
performing pure deeds, and full of reverence;
Such a bhikkhu indeed is called "one who is contentious.
The Cūḷasaṅgāma Sutta is finished.
Its summary verse:
One should ask with a humble mind;
[one should show] respect for the Saṅgha, not for an individual.
The summary [is given] for the purpose of reconciling the Sutta and for the support of the Vinaya,
in the Cūḷasaṅgāma.
This is what is called "a single recitation."
